desc:
The bitwise OR of a non-empty subset is the OR of all of its elements. Among all non-empty subsets of nums (chosen by position, so equal values at different positions count as different choices), the largest OR value that any subset can reach is the OR of the whole array.

Return how many non-empty subsets have an OR equal to that largest value.
hints: Take the OR of the entire array first: that is the target value, and no subset can exceed it.
You can try all 2<sup>n</sup> subsets with an include/skip recursion carrying the running OR. For n = 24 that is slow; look for repeated states.
Many different subsets have the same OR. Keep a map or_value -> number of subsets and update it for every element, instead of enumerating subsets.
editorial: The maximum is M = nums[0] | nums[1] | .... Direct backtracking carries the running OR and counts the leaves with OR equal to M, in O(2n). That is acceptable for n around 16 but too slow for 24.

Because every value is below 214, the OR of any subset is one of at most 16,384 numbers, far fewer than the number of subsets. Keep cnt[v] = number of subsets (including the empty one) whose OR is exactly v, starting from {0: 1}. For each element x, every existing state v either ignores x (stays) or takes it (adds cnt[v] to cnt[v | x]), so update from a snapshot of the old table. The answer is cnt[M]; the empty subset has OR 0 < M and is never counted. This runs in O(n · distinct ORs).
